valuation.title: Inventory 5 — Valuation & the Stock Ledger
valuation.desc: The money layer of stock: what valuation is and where cost is born, moving average and FIFO mechanics, choosing and keeping a method, how every document writes value, negative stock as poison, backdating and revaluation governance, and the remediation craft.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Valuation: where quantity meets money
lessons.html:
Module 1 promised that every warehouse balance is also a naira figure; this module is HOW. Valuation is the machinery that attaches a cost to every unit from the moment it arrives, carries that cost through every movement, and releases it into the profit calculation the moment the unit sells — and understanding it turns three kinds of mystery into arithmetic.

The three numbers valuation produces. The stock asset: every item-at-warehouse quantity times its carried cost, summed — the balance sheet's inventory line, and the number module 4's counting verified the QUANTITY half of. COGS: when goods sell, their carried cost leaves stock and becomes cost of goods sold — the number margin subtracts. Margin itself: revenue minus COGS is only as true as the cost the goods carried — which is the sentence that makes this module commercial rather than clerical: valuation correctness IS margin correctness. Every valuation error in this module's bestiary — the selling-price opening, the zero-rate ghost, the negative-stock corruption — surfaces to the owner as margins that lie, and the consultant who can walk from a strange margin report back through COGS to the ledger entry that poisoned it is worth their fee that day.

Where cost comes from. The carried cost is BORN at arrival: the Purchase Receipt's rate (the PO's committed rate travelling — Procurement 5's protection) plus the landed allocations (Procurement 6's voucher) — the full acquisition truth, written into the ledger entry the day possession happens. Every later movement either CARRIES that cost (transfers — the goods cost what they cost regardless of the room), RELEASES it (deliveries, issues, write-offs — value out at the carried figure), or ADJUSTS it deliberately (the governed exceptions of Chapter 7). Nothing in ordinary trade re-decides cost after arrival — which is why the gates mattered so much, and why this module keeps pointing backward: valuation is not a month-end calculation; it is the gate disciplines, compounded.

The two methods, introduced. When identical units arrived at different costs (January's carton at ₦9,400, March's at ₦9,600) and one sells, which cost leaves? The method answers: moving average blends every arrival into one evolving rate per item-warehouse and releases at the blend (Chapter 2); FIFO keeps each arrival as its own cost layer and releases oldest-first (Chapter 3). Both are honest; they distribute the same total cost differently across time; and the choice, its trade-offs, and the law that you keep it once chosen are Chapter 4's business. What both share — and what this chapter wants permanent — is the writing moment: valuation is written at the moment of movement, entry by entry, and every report merely reads what the movements wrote.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Moving average: the blend
lessons.html:
The moving average is the workhorse method of Nigerian trading implementations, and its mechanics fit in one worked example — which you should be able to reproduce on a whiteboard for any client, because you will.

The worked example. PARA-500 at Central, empty. Receipt one: 100 cartons at ₦9,400 → balance 100, value ₦940,000, average ₦9,400. Receipt two: 200 cartons at ₦9,600 → balance 300, value ₦940,000 + ₦1,920,000 = ₦2,860,000, average ₦9,533.33 — the blend: total value over total quantity, recomputed at every receipt. A delivery of 120: goods leave at the current average — COGS ₦1,144,000 (120 × ₦9,533.33), balance 180, value ₦1,716,000, average unchanged at ₦9,533.33 (issues never move the average; only arrivals at a different rate do). Receipt three: 100 at ₦9,850 (the backup distributor) → balance 280, value ₦2,701,000, average ₦9,646.43. The rate is a living number, drifting with every purchase toward the current market — which is exactly its virtue and its vice.

The virtues. Smoothness: COGS moves gradually, margins do not jump between two sales of identical goods, and the single per-item-warehouse rate is easy to read, quote, and reason about (the valuation rate on any bin IS the item's cost, full stop). Simplicity of story: for owners and their accountants, one number per item that means what our stock of this costs us, blended is an honest and communicable truth. For the price-volatile Nigerian supply environment, the blend also does quiet good work: FX-driven cost jumps enter the margin picture gradually rather than as a cliff between two invoices.

The vices — and their management. The blend has no memory: once a rate enters, it disperses into every subsequent unit's cost, so a single bad receipt poisons the whole stream — the ₦94,000 keyed as ₦940,000 (the decimal slip), the zero-rate entry, the selling-price contamination — and the poison cannot be picked back out; it can only be diluted by future receipts or corrected by supervised revaluation (Chapter 7). The defence is upstream, and you already own every piece: the committed rate travelling untouched (maintain-same-rate), the landed voucher completing it, the last-paid drift eye (Procurement 2) that flags a receipt rate wildly off the item's history BEFORE it blends, and value thresholds on the odd documents that assert rates by hand. The blend also hides vintage: January's cheap stock and March's dear stock become indistinguishable in cost terms, so per-batch profitability questions need batch-level valuation granularity where the firm wants them (module 3's note, now with its mechanism), and slow-moving stock silently carries a partly-modern rate.

Reading a moving-average ledger. The diagnostic skill: the item's valuation-rate HISTORY over time (each receipt's incoming rate against the evolving average) is a chart that confesses everything — the stable gentle drift of a healthy item, the cliff of a bad entry, the sawtooth of alternating suppliers, the slow decay toward zero of an item receiving free or misvalued stock. When margins on an item look wrong, this chart is the first thing you pull, and the entry where the line breaks is usually the whole answer.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — FIFO: the queue of cost layers
lessons.html:
First-In-First-Out keeps what the average blends away: each arrival's cost stays intact as a LAYER, and issues consume the queue oldest-first. The same worked example, the other method.

The worked example, re-run. PARA-500 at Central, empty. Receipt one: 100 at ₦9,400 → layer A [100 @ 9,400]. Receipt two: 200 at ₦9,600 → queue: [100 @ 9,400], [200 @ 9,600]; balance 300, value ₦2,860,000 — same total as the average method, differently organised. The delivery of 120: FIFO consumes oldest-first — all 100 of layer A (₦940,000) plus 20 of layer B (₦192,000): COGS ₦1,132,000 (vs the average's ₦1,144,000 — same goods, same total cost pool, different timing of release). Queue now: [180 @ 9,600]. Receipt three: 100 at ₦9,850 → [180 @ 9,600], [100 @ 9,850]. Every layer keeps its identity until consumed; the item's total value is the sum of its layers; and the difference between methods is never the total cost — it is WHEN each naira of it reaches COGS.

The virtues. Vintage honesty: old cost leaves first, so COGS tracks the sequence in which money was actually spent, and in steadily-rising-cost environments FIFO's COGS runs cooler than the average's while stock value runs warmer (the remaining layers are the recent, dearer ones) — a difference the accountant cares about and the consultant should be able to explain in exactly that sentence. Layer visibility: the queue itself is information (how much of the balance is old-cost vs new-cost), and it harmonises conceptually with FEFO's physical discipline — first in, first out, in cost as on the shelf — though the two are INDEPENDENT systems (FEFO picks batches by expiry; FIFO releases cost by arrival order; they usually agree and nothing breaks when they don't).

The vices. The reading burden: no single rate summarises the item — the bin's rate is an average of surviving layers that changes as they consume, which confuses exactly the people the moving average's one-number story serves; and diagnostics walk layers rather than a line. Sensitivity to sequence: FIFO's correctness depends on entry ORDER even more than the average's does, so backdating and out-of-sequence posting (Chapter 7) disturb it more visibly — the same discipline, higher stakes.

What both methods refuse. Neither method lets ANYONE choose which cost a particular sale carries: the method is an algorithm, not a menu, and the temptation it forecloses is real — the hand-picked cost that flatters this month's margin is precisely what a method's consistency exists to prevent. Where a firm genuinely needs unit-level cost truth (the serialized chiller carrying ITS landed cost to ITS sale), serial-level valuation granularity provides it as architecture, not as discretion — the identity decision and the costing decision converging one more time.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Choosing the method — and keeping it
lessons.html:
Two honest methods, one choice, and a law about the choice: this chapter is the decision's anatomy and its governance.

The decision's owners. The valuation method is an ACCOUNTING POLICY — the accountant (and where applicable the auditor) owns the choice; the consultant owns making its operational consequences vivid and its configuration correct. The conversation the consultant facilitates: how the two methods time cost release (the Chapter 2-3 examples, on the whiteboard), what each does to margins in a rising-cost environment, what the team can operationally sustain (the average's one-number story vs FIFO's layer reading), and what the firm's reporting jurisdictionally requires — the last being the accountant's sentence to finish, not yours.

The practical defaults, honestly stated. For the Nigerian trading and pharmacy clients this curriculum serves, the moving average is the common choice and a defensible default: volatile input costs smooth into readable margins, the single rate communicates, and the operational literacy demands are lower — with the blend's vices managed by the upstream defences Chapter 2 listed. FIFO earns its place where vintage matters commercially (thin-margin distribution where cost timing IS the business), where the accountant's reporting stance prefers it, or where layer visibility answers questions the firm actually asks. Neither is a wrong answer; an UNMADE choice is — the default accepted without the conversation is an accounting policy adopted by accident, and Buying Settings' constitution logic applies here at full strength: the method field is the most consequential default in the stock system.

The consistency law. Once chosen, the method is KEPT: applied to all items it governs (per-item variations exist for structural reasons — the serialized equipment on unit-level valuation beside the averaged consumables — but never as mood), applied across periods, and CHANGED only as a formal accounting event — accountant-led, effective-dated, disclosed where reporting requires, with the transition's revaluation computed and documented. The conviction underneath: method-flipping mid-year is margin manipulation's favourite costume, because each flip re-times cost release and a well-timed flip manufactures a good quarter — which is exactly why auditors treat method changes as events and why the consultant NEVER flips a method to make a report look right. The ticket that asks for it (margins look bad — can we switch to FIFO?) is answered with the diagnosis chapter: margins look wrong because of an ENTRY, almost always, and the entry is findable; the method is not the suspect.

Granularity decisions ride along. The same conversation settles valuation's RESOLUTION: plain item-warehouse level (the default), batch-level where per-lot cost truth earns its keep (import vintages, the discounted-old-stock margin question), serial-level for the individually-valued unit. Each step up buys cost precision and costs bookkeeping — the identity architecture's economics, third appearance — and the choice is made at setup with the ten-year view, beside the flags it mirrors.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — How every document writes value
lessons.html:
Valuation is written at the moment of movement — so here is every movement, and what each one writes. This chapter is the reference card the rest of the module leans on.

  • Purchase Receipt — value IN, born: quantity at the PO's rate, completed by the Landed Cost Voucher's allocations (which ADJUST the received entries' valuation after the fact — the one routine case of post-hoc adjustment, and it is document-governed). This entry is the most consequential valuation write in the system: every later cost is downstream of it.
  • Delivery Note (and sales returns) — value OUT at the method's figure: the average, or the consumed layers. This write IS the COGS of the eventual sale; the return reverses at the value that left (the round-trip law from the trading tracks, now visible as valuation mechanics).
  • Material Issue / write-off — value out at the method's figure, landing as expense where the attribution directs (Inv 2). The write-off's naira cost is this write.
  • Material Receipt — value in at the ASSERTED rate (Inv 2's discipline: derived, not invented) — the entry with no upstream document to inherit from, which is exactly why its rate deserved thresholds and second eyes.
  • Transfers (one- and two-step) — value TRAVELS: out of the source and into the destination (and through transit) at the carried figure. A transfer never revalues — restated here because the mechanics now show why: no acquisition happened, so no new cost exists to write. (Inter-COMPANY movement is different terrain — that is a sale and a purchase wearing transfer clothes, with its own pricing; flag it, don't improvise it.)
  • Stock Reconciliation — the adjustment valued at the method's current figure for shortfalls (loss out at carried cost) and at the carried or asserted rate for surpluses; and — handled with gloves — the reconciliation CAN assert rates, which makes it the deliberate revaluation's instrument (Chapter 7) and the accidental revaluation's favourite accident (module 4's warning about the careless rate column, now with its full mechanism visible).
  • Repack — conservation: outputs at the inputs' total value, allocated (Inv 2). No value created by changing the box; the write just reorganises it.

The read side. Reports never write valuation; they SUM it: the stock balance's value column, the warehouse-wise value (module 1's MD page), the stock ledger's running value per item, and — the bridge report — the stock-to-accounts reconciliation: the ledger's total stock value against the balance sheet's stock account, which should agree continuously and whose divergence is always a specific, findable set of entries (the accountant's month-end friend, and the consultant's first stop when the books and the stock module disagree). Every mystery in this module resolves by finding WHICH WRITE went wrong — and this card is the list of suspects.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Negative stock: the poison
lessons.html:
Now the module's sternest conviction. Negative stock — the ledger driven below zero, selling or issuing what the system does not hold — is not an inconvenience to be tolerated; it is poison to the valuation layer, and this chapter is why, where it comes from, and the posture.

Why it poisons. Valuation releases cost from stock that EXISTS: the average has a rate because value and quantity are both present; FIFO has layers because arrivals were recorded. Drive the quantity below zero and the method must invent a cost for goods it never received — the negative-moment entries carry a fabricated or stale rate, and when the real receipt finally posts, the reconciliation between fiction and fact lands somewhere: rates jump, value totals diverge from quantity truth, and the stock-to-accounts bridge (Chapter 5) starts drifting. One item going negative for a day is a small wound; a firm TRADING on negative stock for months — selling ahead of posting receipts as habit — accumulates valuation damage that no single correction fixes: the SLOT-class remediation (Chapter 8's vignette) is what years of it look like, and it is measured in consultant-months.

The allow-negative setting. The system offers a switch: allow negative stock. The posture: OFF is the default and the discipline — the refusal to sell what the ledger does not hold is the system telling the truth at the moment of temptation, and every refusal is a prompt to post the missing reality (the receipt sitting unentered, the transfer never received) BEFORE trading on it. The honest exceptions are narrow and eyes-open: the go-live transition window (trading must continue while history loads — bounded, dated, and closed), and certain fast-trade configurations where the operational reality (goods sold from the truck before paperwork lands) is a deliberate, accountant-acknowledged model with a same-day posting discipline that keeps negatives to hours. What the setting must never be: flipped on to make an error message go away — the Buying Settings conviction verbatim, because the error message IS the control, and silencing it converts a visible posting problem into an invisible valuation problem.

Where negatives come from — the causes, in order. Unposted receipts (the goods arrived, sold briskly, the receipt queued — the dominant cause, and the fix is gate discipline plus posting-same-day culture); wrong-warehouse sales (the till selling from a leaf that never held the goods — module 1's defaults and restrictions are the fix); sequence errors (the receipt posted, but DATED after the sales it should have preceded — chronology, Chapter 7's terrain); and genuine model mismatches (the van-sales trade whose flows were never designed — a design conversation, not a toggle).

The response drill. A negative flag is a same-day item: identify the missing or mis-dated reality (the ledger walk — the negative moment is visible as the exact entry that crossed zero), post the truth IN ORDER (the receipt with its honest date; the correcting transfer), and let the recompute settle; then the cycle-count trigger (module 4 wired it: negative-stock flags are counted the day they appear) verifies the physical truth the paperwork now matches. What the drill never does: reconcile the negative away by typing a counted quantity over it — the quantity heals and the poisoned rates remain, which is the half-fix that makes SLOT-class messes archaeologically fascinating and commercially expensive.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Backdating & the revaluation ripple
lessons.html:
The ledger is a chronology, and valuation compounds along it — so entries inserted INTO history, and rates changed AFTER the fact, both ripple forward. This chapter is the two governed exceptions to the past is written: the backdated entry and the deliberate revaluation.

The backdating ripple, mechanically. Post a receipt dated the 3rd into a ledger already trading through the 10th, and everything recomputes from the 3rd forward: the average re-blends from that point (every issue between the 3rd and 10th re-releases at the corrected rate), FIFO re-queues its layers, COGS for the intervening sales changes, and the value totals as-at every intervening date shift. The system performs this recompute correctly — the machinery is built for it — but CORRECT is not the same as FREE: reports already circulated now disagree with the ledger's revised truth, a closed month's figures move if the date crosses a period boundary, and repeated casual backdating makes the ledger a document that will not sit still. The governance therefore: backdating is LEGITIMATE for late paperwork posted with its honest date (the truth belongs on the day it happened — Inv 2's law), BOUNDED by the accounting period discipline (entries into closed periods are the accountant's decision, not the storekeeper's convenience — period closing exists precisely to freeze what has been reported), and BATCHED thoughtfully (the month-end sweep that posts a week of stragglers knowingly, at once, with the accountant aware, beats the daily drizzle of surprises).

Deliberate revaluation — the supervised exercise. Sometimes carried costs are WRONG at scale and must be corrected: the selling-price opening discovered late (module 4's disaster, in its remediation phase), the systematic rate error, the accountant-mandated write-down of impaired stock (the aged lot carried above its recoverable value — a policy call with accounting rules behind it). The instrument is the rate-asserting reconciliation (Chapter 5) or the dedicated revaluation entry per the setup — and the governance is the whole point: accountant-LED (the P&L impact of revaluation lands as a gain or loss, and where it lands is their call), effective-DATED deliberately (the ripple is chosen, not stumbled into), DOCUMENTED as an exercise (what was wrong, what evidence set the new rates, what the impact was — the file the auditor will read), and RARE (a firm revaluing routinely has an upstream discipline problem wearing an accounting costume).

The consultant's boundary, drawn plainly. You will be asked to just fix the rates — by clients, by their staff, sometimes urgently. The boundary: mechanical corrections of specific erroneous ENTRIES (the decimal-slip receipt, cancel-and-amend through the document trail) are implementation work; VALUATION POLICY — revaluations, write-downs, method transitions, closed-period entries — is accounting work you execute WITH the accountant, never instead of them. The consultant who reprices a client's stock asset on their own authority has assumed a liability they are not insured for; the one who frames the finding, quantifies the impact, and hands the accountant the decision with the tooling ready is doing the job at its professional grade — and this distinction, held consistently, is also what makes your findings trusted when it matters.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: the valuation year — and the remediation
lessons.html:
Two stories: HealthTrade's healthy year, and the prospect whose system shows what years of broken valuation look like. Together they are this module's before-and-after.

HealthTrade's year (Ch. 1-7). The method hour: moving average chosen with the accountant — volatile input costs, a team that reads one number well, batch-level granularity enabled for the import lines where vintage margins matter (the January $6.20 container vs March's dearer one now answer did the old stock's discount still make money? — yes, by 6 points). The blend defended: month five, a receipt keyed at ₦96,000 against a ₦9,600 history — the last-paid drift eye flags it BEFORE submission (Procurement 2's control, protecting Chapter 2's vice); the decimal slip dies in Draft, the blend never tastes it. One negative incident: a Friday flag on cough syrup at Abeokuta — the ledger walk shows the negative moment at Thursday's till; the cause is a transfer received Thursday PHYSICALLY but posted Friday (sequence, not loss); the receipt is posted with its honest Thursday date, the recompute settles, the trigger count confirms the shelf, and the posting-same-day rule gets a branch refresher. Allow-negative stays OFF; the refusal did its job by making the gap loud. Month-end, every month: the stock-to-accounts bridge agrees to the naira; the accountant's close takes the hour it should.

The remediation vignette (Ch. 6-7) — what you walk into. A prospect asks for help: our stock figures make no sense. The diagnostic hour on their old system finds the classic archaeology: allow-negative ON for four years (switched on in week two to silence an error); hundreds of items with negative-moment histories; Material Receipts at supplier-like rates (the side-door trading of Inv 2, confirmed); opening stock keyed at selling prices in year one and never corrected; the stock-to-accounts bridge divergent by ₦38m and growing; margins that swing 20 points month to month on stable trade. The remediation shape — weeks, sequenced, priced honestly: freeze the bleeding (allow-negative off, the lawful flows restored, posting-same-day instituted — no remediation survives ongoing poisoning); establish quantity truth (the full count, module 4's run-book — valuation cannot be repaired on fictional quantities); establish rate truth (honest costs sourced item by item — purchase records, landed files, the module 4 opening discipline performed years late); the supervised revaluation (accountant-led, effective-dated, documented — the stock asset restated, the P&L impact landed where they direct); and the bridge reconciled going forward, monthly, as the certificate the repair held. The vignette's lesson for the certification: every element of the remediation is a module of this track performed in reverse — which is why the firms that keep these laws never meet this consultant engagement, and why the consultant who holds this track can scope, price, and deliver it when a firm that didn't keeps calling.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fifth law
lessons.html:
The valuation layer's scar tissue — the diseases that surface as margins nobody believes. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — trading on negatives. Symptom: allow-negative on; items living below zero; rate jumps when receipts finally post; the bridge drifting. Disease: the poison normalised (Ch. 6) — fictional cost invented at every negative moment. Fix: the setting off, the causes worked (unposted receipts, wrong-warehouse, sequence), the same-day drill, and where years have passed, the full remediation sequence — never the half-fix.

Pattern 2 — the count as revaluation. Symptom: valuation rates shifting at every reconciliation; nobody meant to reprice anything. Disease: the rate column typed on ordinary count adjustments (Ch. 5; module 4's warning) — quantity corrections performing accidental revaluations. Fix: the rate column asserts nothing on ordinary counts; rate assertion reserved for the supervised exercise with its governance.

Pattern 3 — the casual backdate. Symptom: reports that will not sit still; closed months moving; the accountant at war with the warehouse. Disease: chronology treated as a suggestion (Ch. 7). Fix: honest dates always, period discipline enforced (closed is closed, exceptions accountant-owned), the straggler sweep batched and announced.

Pattern 4 — the method flip. Symptom: a method change lands suspiciously near a bad quarter. Disease: cost-release timing used as makeup (Ch. 4). Fix: the consistency law — changes as formal accounting events only, and the margin complaint answered by diagnosis (find the entry) rather than by switching algorithms.

Pattern 5 — the zero-rate and the decimal slip. Symptom: an item's margin goes brilliant or catastrophic overnight. Disease: one bad rate entered the stream — the free-goods zero, the misplaced decimal, the selling-price contamination (Ch. 2, and modules 2 and 4's gates). Fix: the drift eye at entry, thresholds on rate-asserting documents, and when one lands anyway — the rate-history chart to find it, the document trail to correct it, the accountant where the impact crossed periods.

Pattern 6 — the unread bridge. Symptom: the books and the stock module disagree discovered at year-end, by the auditor. Disease: the stock-to-accounts reconciliation never run (Ch. 5) — divergence compounding unread for months. Fix: the bridge monthly at close, divergences chased to their entries while they are one month old, and the agreement itself filed as the close's certificate.

The fifth law. Module 1: the tree is the map of custody. Module 2: stock moves only by documents. Module 3: identity is operational. Module 4: the count is a dialogue. This module: valuation is written at the moment of movement — every unit carries its honest cost from the day it arrives, and margin truth is nothing but this discipline compounded. Guard the writing moments, refuse the negative, keep the method, govern the exceptions, and read the bridge — and the number the owner cares about most, the margin, becomes a number nobody has to defend, because every kobo of it can be walked back to a document. Three modules remain: the network, the reading, and the structure.

branch_network.title: Inventory 6 — The Branch Network
branch_network.desc: Multi-warehouse trade as a system: the one-stock thesis, the replenishment cycle and run calendar, allocation under scarcity, transit at fleet scale, inter-branch laterals, van and mobile stock disciplines, and branch accountability with the network reads.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — One stock in many rooms
lessons.html:
Everything so far ran in any warehouse; this module is about running MANY — the branch network, which is where your trade's biggest clients live (the 30-branch pharmacy chain, the 100-branch retailer) and where inventory management either becomes a system or becomes a hundred phone calls a day.

The thesis. A network is one stock in many rooms: the firm owns a single pool of inventory that happens to be distributed, and every network decision is a placement decision — WHERE should the pool sit to sell best, move cheapest, and lose least? The two readings of the grid (module 1) become the network's two management questions: the ROLLUP asks do we own enough? (a buying question — Procurement's terrain); the CELLS ask is it in the right rooms? (a placement question — THIS module's terrain, and the one firms confuse with the first constantly: the network that owns plenty while Akure stocks out has a placement problem no purchase order fixes).

The three flows. Every network movement belongs to one of three families, each with its own governance: inbound — the world into central (the Procurement track's whole subject, landing at module 1's receiving defaults: buy centrally, receive centrally, the buying-power architecture); replenishment — central to branches, the network's heartbeat (Chapters 2-4: the requests, the allocation, the runs); and laterals — branch to branch (Chapter 5: legitimate occasionally, diagnostic when chronic). Naming a movement's family names its rules, and the misfiled movement (the branch buying inbound directly, the lateral routed as a return-to-central-and-out-again) is where network discipline first frays.

What scale changes. The mechanics you hold — two-step transfers, transit aging, batch-level receiving — do not change with branch count; what changes is that at scale, EXCEPTIONS become populations: three branches produce the occasional late run; thirty produce a late-run RATE, a transit-shrinkage RATE, a branch-accuracy DISTRIBUTION — and management shifts from handling incidents to reading rates (Chapter 7's whole subject). The other thing scale changes is the cost of informality: the two-site firm survives on the storekeeper phoning the branch; the thirty-site firm phoning is thirty people's full-time job — which is why every rhythm this module installs is a replacement for a phone call, and why the network that runs on its documents scales while the network that runs on its relationships saturates. This is, at network scale, the founder-bottleneck law of the earlier tracks: the system that remembers is what lets the network grow past the people who used to remember it.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The replenishment cycle: the heartbeat
lessons.html:
Replenishment — central to branches, on rhythm — is the network's cardiovascular system, and this chapter is its full cycle from the warehouse's chair (Procurement 3 taught the demand side; here is the fulfilment side, and the join).

The cycle's four beats. Demand lands: branch transfer requests (manual and auto-triggered per branch-level reorder fields), timed to the run calendar — the request layer's machinery, now read as central's inbound worklist, grouped by branch and run. Fulfilment plans: central's picker-planner reads requests against central's OWN position (the four numbers at Central — requests are demand against central's projected, and central's own reorder triggers must see branch demand coming, which is the two-tier planning join: branch triggers fire transfer requests; central's triggers, watching central's projected AS DEPLETED BY those transfers, fire purchase demand — a network that tunes only one tier starves at the other). Where stock covers requests, the plan is the requests; where it does not, Chapter 3's allocation governs. Pick, pack, dispatch: the run's transfers picked per document (batch-picked per FEFO — the network is where FEFO discipline pays or fails at scale, because central picking short-dated stock FIRST to branches is how the whole network's horizon stays healthy), packed per branch with the dispatch documents, and dispatched into transit (Inv 2's two-step, per run). Receive and close: branches receive against dispatches (identity-level — module 3's rule), the transit room clears per run, and the cycle's exceptions (shorts, damages, refusals) resolve by the standing protocols.

The run calendar. Trucks on SCHEDULE — each branch's run days published (Ibadan Tuesdays, Abeokuta Thursdays), requests cut off ahead (the Sunday cutoff for Tuesday's run — honest lead time for picking), and the calendar honoured with the same discipline as every date in these tracks: a network whose runs slip teaches branches to over-request as insurance (the hoarding spiral — padded requests, distorted demand signals, stock parked in the wrong rooms), while a network whose runs are boringly reliable can run LEAN at the branches, because tomorrow's truck is a fact. Run reliability is therefore not logistics housekeeping; it is what makes every branch's stockholding honest — the published calendar, the cutoffs, and the on-time rate READ (Chapter 7 scores it) are the network's equivalent of the supplier OTIF discipline, self-applied.

Pick-pack discipline. The dispatch is a gate (value leaving central's custody), and it gets gate treatment: picked quantities confirmed against the transfer document (not the request — the TRANSFER is what was approved and allocated), batch identities recorded as picked (what left is known by lot — the recall and the swap-catch both depend on it), sealed or secured per run with the seal numbers on the waybill, and the dispatcher's sign-off closing central's custody cleanly. Thirty seconds per line at dispatch is the difference between a transit shortfall investigation that reads documents and one that reads memories.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Allocation under scarcity
lessons.html:
The week arrives when central cannot fill every request — the import delayed, the demand spike, the supplier short-close. What happens next separates governed networks from political ones, and this chapter is the governance.

The failure mode first. Ungoverned scarcity allocates by VOLUME OF VOICE: the branch manager who calls loudest, knows the storekeeper, or escalates to the MD gets filled; the quiet branch stocks out. The damage compounds beyond the week: branches learn that shouting works (the political spiral), request padding becomes rational (the hoarding spiral joins it), and the demand signal — the one input every planning decision feeds on — is now noise. Scarcity is rare; the behaviours it trains are permanent, which is why the policy must exist BEFORE the week that needs it.

The allocation policy — written, like every gate number. The honest bases, chosen per the firm's strategy and encoded: pro-rata by request (each branch gets the same fill percentage — simple, transparent, gameable by padding, so it pairs with request-honesty monitoring); by velocity (fill proportional to each branch's actual sell-through — the stock goes where it sells, which is usually the network-profit-maximising answer and the fairest to honest requesters, since it allocates on recorded sales, not requested hopes); by priority tier (strategic branches — the flagship, the contract-committed location — filled first per a written tier list, then the remainder by the base rule); and for regulated or critical lines, the minimum-cover floor (no branch below a safety threshold of essential items while any other holds surplus — the network's version of triage). Most real policies compose these: floors first, then velocity, tiers documented. What matters less than the formula is that it is WRITTEN, applied visibly, and survives the loud phone call.

The mechanics. Scarce lines flagged at fulfilment planning (requested exceeds available); the policy computes each branch's fill; transfers issue at allocated quantities with the REMAINDER handling honest: the unfilled request balance stays visible (partially-fulfilled requests, the machinery you know) and is either rolled to the next run automatically (the backorder-to-branch) or released when the branch's need lapses — never silently vanished, because a branch whose shortfalls evaporate unexplained returns to the padding spiral. And the COMMUNICATION beat: allocation weeks are announced — what is short, what the policy gave each branch, when relief lands (the incoming PO's date — Procurement 5's honest pipeline earning its keep) — because a branch that understands the week holds its discipline, and one that discovers it at the empty truck does not.

Scarcity as signal. Chronic allocation on a line is not a logistics fact; it is an upstream message: central under-buying (the planning fields conversation), a demand shift the forecast missed, or a supplier problem the scorecard should be catching. The allocation log — which lines, how often, how deep — is the network telling procurement where its model is wrong, and the quarterly read of it closes this loop exactly as the expiry-loss read closed the other one: the warehouse writing letters to the buyers, in numbers.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Transit at fleet scale: runs, waybills & the close-out
lessons.html:
Inv 2 built the two-step and the transit room; at network scale, transit becomes an OPERATION — trucks, runs, drivers, seals — and this chapter is its management layer.

The run as the unit of management. Not the transfer, not the truck-kilometre: the RUN — one vehicle, one date, one or more drop points, a manifest of dispatch documents. Everything reconciles at run level: what left central (the dispatches), what each branch received (the receipts against them), and what remains in transit (which, at run close-out, should be exactly zero). The multi-drop run — one truck, three branches — is the scale pattern: dispatches SPLIT per destination from the start (three transfer documents, one per branch, never one blob to be divided roadside — the roadside division is where quantities go to become disputes), loaded in reverse-drop order, and each drop's receipt closing its own document while the run's remainder rides on.

The paper of the road. The waybill/manifest carries: the run's dispatch document references, quantities by drop, seal numbers where sealing is used (the seal intact at the branch converts the count conversation — an intact seal with a short count points inside central's packing; a broken seal points at the road — cheap forensics, applied before blame), the driver's acknowledgment of the load (the road's custody has a name — the driver signed for what the documents say, which is both the accountability and the driver's own protection, module 1's custodian framing on wheels), and each branch's signed receipt annotation. The paper is thirty seconds per drop and it is the entire difference between a shortfall investigation and a shortfall argument.

The close-out. Every run CLOSES, same-day or next-morning: all drops' receipts posted, the transit room's run balance at zero, exceptions logged (shorts, damages, refusals — a branch may refuse a damaged carton at its gate exactly as central refuses a supplier's: the refusal rides the paper home and resolves through quarantine or write-off from transit, never through quiet absorption). The unclosed run is the aging read's raw material (Inv 2's smoke detector), and the close-out discipline is what keeps the detector silent: a network of daily runs with same-day close-outs has a transit room that breathes — full by afternoon, empty by morning — and any standing balance is, by construction, an incident with a run number attached.

Driver and fleet accountability, read as rates. At scale (Chapter 1's law), transit performance becomes population statistics: shortfall rate by driver and by route, damage rate by run type, on-time rate against the calendar — read monthly, managed like any custody. The honest framing for the team: the documented run protects the driver whose loads arrive whole (the rate proves it), exactly as it exposes the pattern that needs a conversation — and the seals-counts-signatures ritual, sold as protection rather than suspicion, is adopted; sold as surveillance, it is gamed. Where third-party haulage carries runs, the same paper governs and the rates feed the haulier conversation — a supplier scorecard for the road, because that is what it is.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Inter-branch laterals: the exception with a message
lessons.html:
Branch-to-branch transfers — Ibadan sending stock to Akure directly — are the network's pressure valve: legitimate in the moment, diagnostic in the pattern, and worth a chapter precisely because both halves are true.

The legitimate lateral. The genuine cases: the local spike one branch can cover faster than central's next run (the weekend event, the clinic's bulk ask), the imbalance correction cheaper than a round trip (Ibadan long, Akure short, and the direct road shorter than two runs through Lagos), and the slow-mover rebalance (Chapter 7's dead-stock work often ends in laterals — the stock that will not sell HERE moving to where it does). The mechanics are nothing new: the two-step transfer, branch to branch, with transit custody, identity-level receiving, and the run paper — a lateral is a small run and gets run treatment; the one-step lateral across a real road is the same conviction as ever.

The governance. Laterals move stock OUTSIDE the planned flows, so they carry light but real governance: policy states who may initiate (branch managers propose; central approves above a threshold — because central owns the placement picture, and a lateral that solves Ibadan's Saturday may be robbing the allocation plan's Tuesday); visibility is mandatory (every lateral visible to central as it happens — the network's placement map must include the moves it didn't plan); and the receiving branch counts like any gate (branch-to-branch familiarity is exactly where counting discipline dies first — the two managers who trust each other, until the variance neither can explain).

The economics, taught honestly. A lateral moves stock TWICE (central→Ibadan→Akure) and costs twice — freight, handling, transit risk, and days of shelf absence — so the lateral that looks free at the branch level is the network paying double for a placement it got wrong once. This is not an argument against laterals (the second move is often cheaper than the stockout it prevents); it is the argument for reading them as PRICED decisions: the approval threshold exists so someone weighs the double-move against the alternative (wait for the run; expedite from central; let the sale go), and the lateral log carries the cost the network chose to pay.

The pattern as diagnosis. One lateral is weather; a lateral RATE is climate — and chronic laterals on a corridor are the network confessing a systematic error: Akure chronically importing from Ibadan means Akure's allocation or reorder fields are set for a smaller branch than Akure has become (the growth the planning never heard — retune the fields), or central's run frequency to Akure is too sparse for its velocity (the calendar conversation), or the demand forecast is systematically placing stock one branch west of where it sells. The quarterly lateral read — corridors, lines, values, stated reasons — is the placement model's error report, and the mature network treats a falling lateral rate as the success metric it is: the network that plans well moves everything once.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Van & mobile stock: the warehouse on wheels
lessons.html:
Route trade — the van selling to kiosks and shops along a route, the market-day mobile stall — is a Nigerian distribution staple, and its inventory truth stands on one idea: the van is a warehouse. A leaf, a custodian, a daily cycle — and this chapter is the cycle's discipline.

The daily cycle, three beats. Load-out: morning transfer from the branch/central leaf INTO the van's leaf — counted at the tailgate by the van custodian (their custody begins here, and their signature accepts exactly what the document says: the count-before-sign law at the smallest gate in the network), stocked per the route's plan (the van's load is a placement decision like any other — the route's demand history sets it, not the driver's optimism). The route: sales made FROM the van's warehouse through the sales machinery (the van is the source leaf on every sale — module 1's defaults wiring the van user to their van), cash or transfer per the trade's terms, returns and refusals riding back in the van's custody. Evening reconciliation — the beat that makes or breaks van trade: load-out = sales + returns + remaining stock, counted at the tailgate, same day, every day. The arithmetic closes or it does not; a gap is named TONIGHT (short stock = the day's shrinkage, on this van, this route, this custodian — investigated while the day is memorable) — and the van that reconciles daily has shrinkage in kobo while the van that reconciles weekly has it in cartons, because the leak on wheels compounds faster than any warehouse leak: small quantities, cash proximity, zero oversight between tailgates.

The van custodian's number. Module 1's framing at its sharpest: the van driver-seller holds company stock AND often company cash, alone, all day — the highest-trust custody per naira in the network — and the daily reconciliation is what makes that trust STRUCTURAL: the custodian who closes clean every evening has a record that promotes them; the discipline protects the honest exactly as it exposes the leak. Van shrinkage is read per van, per route, per custodian (the rates law again), and the route rotation — custodians periodically swapped across routes — separates route-shrinkage (the risky market, the theft-prone stop) from custodian-shrinkage (the pattern that travels with the person): cheap analytics, decisive conversations.

Identity and expiry on wheels. The van carries batch-tracked goods, so the disciplines ride along, sized to the tailgate: load-outs record batches loaded (the van's FEFO is loaded-first-sold-first by shelf discipline in the van), evening remainders confirm by lot where the trade's risk warrants it, and the van's stock ages like any room's — the route stock that rides for weeks is the horizon's business too. Where the trade is fast and the items low-risk, the batch discipline lightens deliberately (policy, not neglect) — proportionality, as everywhere.

Van economics in the network reads. The van is a branch in miniature and reads like one: value carried, sales per route-day, shrinkage rate, reconciliation-clean streak — the per-van page beside the per-branch page in Chapter 7's dashboard. And the design note for implementations: van leaves are cheap; create one PER VEHICLE (never a pooled Vans warehouse — pooled custody is no custody, the module 1 law that a place answers to a person), default-wired to the van's user, restricted hard, and reconciled on the daily rhythm from day one — because van trade retrofitted onto discipline after a bad quarter is the hardest retrofit in this track.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Branch accountability & the network reads
lessons.html:
Scale turns incidents into rates (Chapter 1), and this chapter is the reading room: the per-branch scorecard, the network dashboard, and the rhythm that turns thirty rooms into one managed system.

The branch scorecard. Per branch, per period, the custody vitals — every one of them a number earlier modules taught this track to produce: stock value held (the custodian's number — module 1); count accuracy rate (module 4's cycle programme, per branch); shrinkage rate (module 4's read, the custody comparison); expiry/markdown losses (module 3's horizon, per branch — the branch that lets stock age is visible beside the one that works its ladder); transit performance (receiving discipline: receipts posted same-day, identity-level, exceptions resolved — module 2 and Chapter 4); request honesty (requested vs sold — the padding detector, Chapter 3's spiral watched); and stockout incidence (the placement failure the whole network exists to prevent). Weighted per the firm's values and read quarterly WITH the branch manager — the supplier scorecard's exact logic pointed inward: conversations from records, praise specific, problems specific, and the standings mapped to real consequences (the clean branch earns autonomy — lighter approval thresholds, first-tier allocation; the struggling one earns support first and scrutiny second, in that order, because most branch problems are training and staffing problems wearing discipline costumes).

The network dashboard. The rollup page, read weekly by whoever runs the network: total stock by room family (branches, central, transit, quarantine, vans — the logical rooms' balances in one row), the placement heat (stockouts and overstocks by branch — the two failure modes of one placement question), transit health (unclosed runs, aging), the allocation log's active lines, the lateral rate, and the exceptions aging (unresolved shortfalls, open investigations). One page; every number a drill-down into machinery this track built; and the page's job is the same as every reading rhythm in these tracks — surprises prevented, trends caught at two data points instead of eight.

The branch manager's weekly page. The same truths, scoped to one room, pushed TO the branch (not pulled by head office only — a scorecard the branch sees moves behaviour; one it discovers at review time breeds resentment): my stock value, my accuracy, my shrinkage, my expiring lines this month, my unreceived transfers, my scorecard trend. The transparency is the management system: branch managers who see their numbers weekly manage them daily, and the network conversation shifts from inspection to coaching — which at thirty branches is the only conversation there is time for.

The reads close every loop. Notice what this chapter's numbers feed: allocation logs to procurement (Chapter 3), expiry losses to buying (module 3), lateral rates to placement planning (Chapter 5), shrinkage distributions to security and training (module 4), transit rates to fleet and hauliers (Chapter 4). The network read is not a report ABOUT the system; it is the system's nervous system — and the final module will consolidate every rhythm this track has installed into the calendar that keeps it read.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade opens Akure
lessons.html:
Branch three. The network's playbook, executed — every chapter clocking in.

The opening playbook (Ch. 1; modules 1, 4). Before a naira of stock moves: the leaves created (Akure Store, Akure Quarantine — named to pattern, parented under Branches), defaults wired (Akure's sales default from Akure Store; rejections to its quarantine), users restricted to their leaves plus read-on-Central, branch reorder fields set from the business plan's velocity estimates (flagged for aggressive retuning at 90 days — opening estimates are always wrong; the discipline is knowing it and scheduling the correction). The opening stock arrives as a TRANSFER, not a purchase — the network buys centrally (the architecture holding at its first temptation: the local wholesaler's opening deal politely declined) — dispatched as a dedicated run, received identity-level by the new team as their first live drill: count, lots, sign. Day one closes with Akure's bins true, its custody signed, and its manager holding the weekly page format they will live on.

The scarcity week (Ch. 3). Month two: Emzor's allocation short-close (the Procurement 5 case study's ripple reaching the network) leaves central 180 cartons against 300 requested across three branches. The policy — floors first, then velocity — computes: every branch to its 30-carton essential floor first, the remainder by trailing 8-week sell-through (Ibadan 58%, Abeokuta 27%, Akure 15% of velocity): Ibadan 87, Abeokuta 51, Akure 42. The allocation is ANNOUNCED with the relief date (the backup distributor's PO, Tuesday week); unfilled balances stay visible on the requests and roll to the relief run. The loudest call of the week — Ibadan's manager, naturally — receives the policy's arithmetic instead of a renegotiation, and the padding spiral never starts. The allocation log opens its first entry; the quarterly read will hand it to procurement.

The van launch (Ch. 6). Month three: Akure's route trade begins — one van, one leaf (Van AK-1), one custodian, wired and restricted. Day one loads out clean, sells, reconciles to the naira at the tailgate. Day two closes ₦9,000 short — named that evening: the arithmetic (load-out 412,000 = sales 366,500 + returns 8,300 + remaining 28,200... short 9,000) is on the table while the day is memorable, and the custodian's own recall finds it: two cough syrup units handed to a kiosk on a pay Friday promise, unrecorded. The resolution: the trade's credit terms are for the SYSTEM to extend, not the tailgate (the sale entered properly against the kiosk's account, the custodian trained, the rule now vivid) — and the day-two catch, handled as training rather than accusation, sets the van's culture: the reconciliation protects everyone, and the clean-close streak starts at day three.

The quarter's network read (Ch. 5, 7). The dashboard at quarter-end: Akure's accuracy 95.1% and climbing (new-team normal), its reorder fields retuned at day 90 as scheduled (velocity ran 22% over plan — the growth heard early because the read existed); one lateral in the quarter (Ibadan→Akure, approved, the spike covered — logged with its double-move cost, no pattern); transit clean (every run closed same-day; one shortfall investigated to a packing miss at central, corrected at the pick discipline); van AK-1's clean streak at 61 days. The scorecards go to the managers before the review, the review runs from the numbers, and the network — three rooms grown to five (two branches became three, plus a van) — still reads on one page. The playbook filed; branch four will take a week.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The network layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — allocation by decibel. Symptom: scarce weeks filled by phone-call order; quiet branches stocking out; requests padding upward every quarter. Disease: no written policy (Ch. 3) — the political and hoarding spirals training permanent behaviour in rare weeks. Fix: the policy composed and encoded (floors, velocity, tiers), applied visibly, announced with relief dates — and the padding detector (requested vs sold) watching the recovery.

Pattern 2 — the chronic corridor. Symptom: the same lateral, month after month; branch managers running a private redistribution economy. Disease: the placement model wrong and nobody reading its error report (Ch. 5) — fields, calendar, or forecast misplacing stock systematically. Fix: the quarterly lateral read; the corridor's root cause retuned; laterals returned to weather from climate.

Pattern 3 — the leak on wheels. Symptom: van stock reconciled weekly or never; shrinkage discovered in cartons; cash and stock gaps entangled. Disease: the daily tailgate arithmetic skipped (Ch. 6) — the highest-risk custody on the lightest discipline. Fix: load-out = sales + returns + remaining, every evening, gaps named same-day; per-van leaves (pooled custody is no custody); route rotation separating route from custodian in the rates.

Pattern 4 — the branch that buys. Symptom: branch petty-cash purchases at retail; local supplier relationships central never met. Disease: the network shape broken at its economics (Ch. 1; the conviction from Procurement 3, seen from the warehouse) — usually CAUSED by unreliable runs or ungoverned allocation, which is the diagnostic point: the branch that buys retail is often escaping a network that failed it. Fix: the run reliability and allocation governance repaired FIRST, then the buying rule re-enforced — discipline demanded only after the system deserves it.

Pattern 5 — runs that never close. Symptom: a transit room with a permanent balance; shortfalls surfacing at branch counts weeks later; drivers blamed by vibe. Disease: no run-level close-out (Ch. 4) — the smoke detector unplugged at scale. Fix: the run as the reconciliation unit, same-day close-outs, the waybill-and-seal paper, and the rates read that replaces vibe with pattern.

Pattern 6 — the unread network. Symptom: head office discovers branch problems at annual stocktake; managers see their numbers at review time, angrily. Disease: the reads never built or never pushed (Ch. 7) — thirty rooms managed as thirty surprises. Fix: the scorecard and the weekly page, pushed to the branch; the dashboard's one page weekly at the centre; consequences mapped so the numbers mean something.

The sixth law. The tree is the map; movements are documents; identity is operational; the count is a dialogue; valuation is written at the moment of movement. This module: the network is one stock in many rooms — move it on schedule, allocate it by policy, reconcile every room to zero, and read the whole on one page. The run calendar is its heartbeat, the allocation policy its fairness, the tailgate arithmetic its smallest gate, and the branch scorecard its memory — and a network that keeps this law grows by playbook while the other kind grows by heroics until the heroes saturate. Two modules remain: the reading, and the structure.
