stock_health.title: Inventory 7 — Stock Health & Analytics
stock_health.desc: The reading module: stock as capital and its vital signs, turns and coverage, aging and the dead-stock ladder, ABC and the value-velocity matrix, stockout and availability tracking, the reports shelf, and the monthly stock health page.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Stock as capital: the vital signs
lessons.html:
Six modules built and defended the stock truth; this module READS it — because stock is not goods on shelves, it is capital wearing inventory's clothes, usually the largest single asset a trading firm owns, and the reading discipline is what makes that capital WORK instead of sit.

The capital framing, taught to owners. The ₦48m at Central is ₦48m the firm chose to hold as stock instead of cash, expansion, or debt reduction — and every stock decision is silently a capital-allocation decision: the overstock is capital parked and depreciating (expiry, obsolescence, storage); the stockout is capital ABSENT from where it earns; the dead pallet is capital in prison. The consultant who opens the analytics conversation with this framing gets the owner's attention immediately, because it converts warehouse reports into money reports — which is what they always were.

Health, defined. Healthy stock is four things at once: the RIGHT AMOUNT (enough to serve, not enough to rot — turns and coverage, Chapter 2), in the RIGHT PLACES (the network's placement question — availability, Chapter 5), MOVING (aging and dead stock, Chapter 3), and TRUE (accuracy and valuation — modules 4-5's certificates, read here as vitals). A firm can fail any one while passing the others — the accurate, well-placed warehouse full of stock that stopped selling; the fast-turning network that stocks out weekly — which is why the health read is a PANEL of vitals, never one number, and Chapter 7 assembles the panel onto its page.

The reads exist because the disciplines exist. Notice what this module does NOT have to build: every number it reads is exhaust from machinery already running — turns from the ledger's movements, aging from its dates, accuracy from module 4's programme, shrinkage from its reason codes, expiry losses from module 3's horizon, availability from the bins. A firm that kept modules 1-6 gets this module's analytics essentially FREE; a firm that did not has reports that read fiction — the garbage-in law that makes analytics the reward for discipline rather than its substitute. When a client asks for better stock reports, the diagnostic question is always whether the reports are weak or the ledger beneath them is — and by this point in the certification you know exactly how to tell.

The cadence law, restated for the reading room. Every report in this module earns a rhythm and an owner or it is decoration (the conviction from three tracks, final appearance): the daily reads are operational (bins, exceptions), the weekly are managerial (the network dashboard's vitals), the monthly is the health page with the MD, the quarterly re-runs the structural analyses (ABC, the matrix). This module supplies the WHAT; the final module's calendar fixes the WHEN and WHO.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Turns & coverage: is the capital working?
lessons.html:
The first vital: how fast stock converts back to cash. Two lenses, one question.

Stock turnover. The ratio: COGS over average stock value for a period (units work too — units sold over average units held — for item-level reads where value distorts). Turns of 12 means the stock pool converts to sales monthly; turns of 2 means the average naira sits six months. The mechanics matter less than the reading discipline: turns are computed PER ITEM and PER WAREHOUSE and then rolled — because the firm-wide number is an average of extremes that hides both diseases (the fast seller masking the dead pallet; Chapter 9 convicts the firm-wide-only read), and the interesting information is always the DISTRIBUTION: which items turn 20, which turn 1, and what each deserves.

Days of cover. The operational twin: current stock over average daily sell-through = how many days the shelf survives at current velocity. Cover is the number planning conversations actually use (the reorder fields of Buying 2 ARE cover targets in disguise: reorder level = lead-time cover plus safety cover), and its per-item-per-warehouse read is the placement dial: Akure holding 9 days of a line while Ibadan holds 60 is the lateral conversation (module 6) wearing arithmetic.

Interpreting both directions. The reading error to train out of clients: HIGH turns are not simply good, LOW not simply bad — each end has a failure mode. Turns too high / cover too thin: the firm is surfing stockout risk — every supply hiccup becomes a lost sale, expediting costs climb, and the apparent efficiency is fragility (the availability read, Chapter 5, is this number's conscience). Turns too low / cover too deep: capital parked — holding cost, expiry exposure (for dated goods, cover beyond remaining shelf life is a write-off on a schedule), and the opportunity cost the capital framing prices. The TARGET is a band, set per category (fast FMCG lines run high turns by nature; slow specialty lines run low legitimately), and the read is exceptions against the band — the item outside its band in either direction is the worklist.

Category benchmarks and the honest comparison. Turns compare only within like: the pharmacy's fast analgesics against ITS fast analgesics over time, branch against branch on the SAME line, the firm against its trade's rough norms where known — never the antibiotic against the generator against the hair cream in one league table. The trend beats the level (the line whose turns halved in two quarters is a story regardless of where it sits), and the decomposition beats both: a falling turn is EITHER slowing sales or growing stock, and the two have different owners — the read that says WHICH (sell-through trend against stock trend, side by side) is the read that assigns the conversation correctly.

What turns feed. Cover targets tune the planning fields (the quarterly exception review of Buying 2, now with its data source named); the turns distribution feeds ABC and the matrix (Chapter 4); thin-cover flags feed availability watch (Chapter 5); deep-cover flags feed the aging read (Chapter 3) before the aging read has to find them the hard way. One ratio, four consumers — which is why it leads the panel.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Aging & the dead-stock ladder
lessons.html:
The second vital: is the stock MOVING? Aging finds the capital that stopped, and the ladder is the discipline that releases it.

The aging read. Stock stratified by time since last movement (last sale or issue — receipts don't count as movement for this purpose; a pallet that only ever arrives is exactly the patient we're looking for): 0-30 days, 31-60, 61-90, 91-180, 180+ — by item, by warehouse, VALUED. The value column is the read's teeth: ₦6.8m has not moved in 90+ days lands differently than a list of SKUs, and per-warehouse stratification catches the network pattern (moving fine at Central, dead at the branch that over-requested it — a rebalance, not a markdown).

Dead stock, defined and owned. The firm writes its definition — no movement in N days (90 for fast trade, 180 for slower; per category where honesty requires) — and the definition creates the WORKLIST: every line past the threshold has an owner and a next action, reviewed monthly. Without the written threshold, dead stock is a vibe discovered annually; with it, a pipeline worked continuously — the module 4 shrinkage logic applied to slowness.

The ladder — every rung cheaper than the next. Module 3's markdown ladder generalised beyond expiry, ordered by value recovered:

  • Push — visibility first: front-of-shelf, staff spiffs, the counter suggestion; costs nothing, works more often than pride expects, and is the honest first test of whether the item is dead or merely hidden.
  • Rebalance — the placement fix: dead HERE may be alive THERE — the lateral (module 6's economics: the double-move priced against the alternative rungs, and usually winning); the network's whole point is that a room's dead stock gets the other rooms' demand for free.
  • Markdown — price against the calendar: the pre-approved discount ladder (the pricing-rule machinery, not per-carton negotiation), stepped down on schedule; for dated goods this IS module 3's ladder, deadline-driven.
  • Bundle & convert — the slow-mover riding the fast one (the bundle machinery from the selling track), or repack into the form that sells (Inv 2 — the bulk that died as cartons living as strips).
  • Liquidate — the bulk exit at honest salvage: the institutional buyer, the trade channel, the clearance event; margin surrendered, capital and shelf recovered.
  • Write off — the governed end (Inv 2's signatures) when the recovery costs more than the recovery; the rung nobody enjoys and delay makes MORE expensive: dated goods rot toward it, storage bleeds toward it, and the ladder's whole arithmetic is that month-one action at ANY rung beats month-twelve write-off at the last one.

The capital-release framing. The ladder's report line is not losses taken but capital released: ₦4.9m of dead value converted back to cash-and-shelf (at whatever recovery each rung achieved) is ₦4.9m re-deployable into stock that turns — and shelf space, in retail, is itself inventory capacity the dead stock was renting for free. Owners who resist markdowns as losses usually accept them as release; the framing is the consultant's tool, and the ladder-progress line on the monthly page (Chapter 7) is where it lives.

Upstream, always. Dead stock is a message with a return address: the buy that misjudged (quantity or item — the planning conversation), the assortment that drifted from the customer, the branch allocation that shipped hope. The quarterly dead-stock cause read — what died and WHY — is the third of this track's letters to procurement, and the firms whose dead-stock rate falls are the ones that answered the mail.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — ABC & the value-velocity matrix
lessons.html:
The third structural read: not every item deserves equal attention, and this chapter is the formal machinery for aiming attention where money and movement actually are.

ABC, mechanically. Items ranked by a period's value contribution (consumption value — quantity moved × cost — is the standard basis; sales value works for commercial lenses); the cumulative curve drawn; the classes cut: A — the vital few (typically ~20% of items carrying ~70-80% of value), B — the middle (~30% of items, ~15-25%), C — the trivial many (~50% of items, ~5-10%). The percentages are conventions, not laws; the SHAPE is the law — every real inventory is this skewed, and the skew is the entire management insight: treat all items equally and you spend 80% of attention on 10% of the money.

What ABC feeds — the consumers you already know. The counting programme (module 4: A monthly, B quarterly, C annually — this chapter is where those classes come from); buying attention (A items get the sourcing rigour, the market tests, the drift eye at full alertness; C items get automation and sensible defaults — the Procurement 4 machinery pointed by class); service levels (A stockouts are emergencies, C stockouts are Tuesday — availability targets set per class, Chapter 5); and master-data care (A items' planning fields reviewed quarterly by name; C items' by exception). One analysis, four consumers — recomputed on a calendar (quarterly or semi-annual: assortments drift, and the ABC computed once in 2019 is Chapter 9's museum piece), with class CHANGES read as news: the C item climbing to B is a trend the buying should hear; the A item sliding is Chapter 3's early warning.

The value-velocity matrix — ABC's second dimension. Value alone misleads: the high-value slow-mover and the high-value fast-mover are both A and need opposite handling. Cross value with VELOCITY (turns, Chapter 2) and read four quadrants:

  • High value, fast — the franchise: guard it (availability first, counting tightest, supplier redundancy per Procurement 1's concentration logic, the drift eye sharpest). Stockouts here are the expensive kind.
  • High value, slow — the danger quadrant: big money sitting — deliberate stockholding only (the genuine specialty line held for strategic reasons, documented) or Chapter 3's patient in the making; reviewed by NAME monthly, cover capped, buying gated.
  • Low value, fast — the automation quadrant: the workhorse tail that runs itself — auto-replenishment tuned and trusted, counting light, attention minimal by DESIGN (the win here is spending nothing managing it).
  • Low value, slow — the pruning quadrant: the assortment's barnacles — the ladder's liquidate-and-delist candidates, the range review's kill list; every SKU here costs master-data care, shelf, and count minutes for near-zero contribution, and the periodic prune is inventory hygiene at the ASSORTMENT level.

The matrix as the buying conversation. One page, four quadrants, every item placed: this is the single most persuasive artefact the warehouse hands the buyer and the owner — it converts we hold too much stock (an argument) into we hold ₦11m in the danger quadrant and here are the twelve items (a worklist). The consultant who builds this page at every engagement builds it because it works.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Stockouts & availability: the other failure
lessons.html:
Every vital so far watched stock that EXISTS; this chapter watches the stock that DOESN'T — the empty shelf, the invisible failure, and the discipline that makes it visible and priced.

Why stockouts hide. Overstock announces itself (the pallet in the aisle, the aging read, the value on the page); the stockout leaves NO RECORD by default — the customer asked, the shelf was empty, the sale never happened, and no ledger line marks the naira that walked out. A firm that reads only its stock reports therefore systematically over-corrects toward leanness (every visible number rewards holding less; the invisible number punishing it is never seen) — and the availability discipline exists to put the missing number on the page.

The two measurements. Zero-balance tracking — the systemic read: days at zero (or below safety floor) per item per warehouse, from the bin history — cheap, automatic, and honest about DURATION (the line that zeroed for three hours vs three weeks); expressed as the availability rate — the percentage of item-days in stock, per branch, per class (the A-class availability target is the one that matters: 98%+ for the franchise quadrant is a common posture; C-class tolerates more). Lost-sale capture — the demand-side read: the counter and POS discipline of recording the ask that couldn't be served (the two-tap not available capture where the till supports it; the counter book where it doesn't) — imperfect by nature, invaluable in pattern: the item asked-for weekly that the assortment never carried is a listing decision the zero-balance read can never surface, because you cannot zero-balance what you never stocked.

Pricing the stockout. The lost sale's cost is the margin forgone — plus the substitution risk (the customer who found it next door and liked next door), which for retail is the expensive part. The framing arithmetic for owners: an A-item stocking out for a week costs its weekly margin CERTAINLY and a customer relationship PROBABLY, and against that price the marginal cost of two more days' cover is usually trivial — which is the availability read disciplining the leanness instinct exactly as the aging read disciplines the hoarding one. The two reads together ARE the placement dial (module 6's language): stockouts say too little or wrong room; aging says too much or wrong room; and the dial is turned per item-warehouse, not per slogan.

The response taxonomy. A stockout's cause assigns its fix: the trigger that never fired (planning fields — retune), the trigger that fired into a phantom pipeline (the stale PO — Procurement 5's sweep), the allocation that shorted the branch (module 6's policy and its relief), the run that slipped (the calendar's on-time read), the demand spike nobody could have held (logged, forgiven, and fed to the forecast), or the supplier failure (the scorecard's evidence). The monthly stockout review — incidents by cause, per branch — is short, and it is the read that turns availability from a percentage into a programme.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The reports shelf: which report answers which question
lessons.html:
The track has named a dozen reads; this chapter is the shelf — organised, as the earlier tracks organised theirs, by the QUESTION each report answers, because a consultant who maps question→report in one breath teaches clients to self-serve.

  • What do we hold, right now? — the stock balance: item × warehouse, quantity and value, the summary snapshot. The first report every client learns, and the one they over-use for questions it cannot answer — it shows the NOW, not the HOW.
  • How did it get this way? — the stock ledger: the history, entry by entry, document by document (module 1's diagnostic superpower, formalised as the second report every consultant opens). Balance surprises decompose here; the pair together (balance for the what, ledger for the why) answer most support tickets before they escalate.
  • What will we hold? — the projected view: the four numbers forward (actual − reserved + incoming), per item-warehouse — the planning read, and the one whose honesty depends on the ghost and phantom sweeps (the corrupted promise corrupts THIS page first).
  • Is it fresh? — the batch and expiry reads (module 3's horizon and batch-wise balances): per-warehouse, worklist-formatted, decision-owned.
  • Is it true? — module 4's accuracy rate and variance trends; module 5's stock-to-accounts bridge — the certificates, read as vitals.
  • Is it working? — this module's panel: turns and cover (Ch. 2), aging and dead stock (Ch. 3), ABC and the matrix (Ch. 4), availability (Ch. 5).
  • Is the network placed right? — module 6's dashboard: transit health, allocation log, lateral rate, branch scorecards.

The shelf's disciplines. Three, all restatements the certification has earned: question first — the report request that cannot name its question is answered with the question, not a report (the custom-report ticket that begins can you add a column usually dissolves when the underlying question meets the existing shelf); cadence and owner — every shelf report carries its rhythm and its name or it decays to decoration (Chapter 1's law; the final module's calendar enforces it); and drill-down over export — the reading culture to build is one where numbers are interrogated in the system (page → line → document — the provenance always three clicks away) rather than exported to spreadsheets where they detach from their evidence and begin their second life as fiction. The firm whose managers drill down argues from documents; the firm whose managers export argues from tabs — and only one of those arguments ends.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The monthly stock health page
lessons.html:
The panel assembles. One page, monthly, owned — the stock system's report card, and the conversation it scripts with the owner.

The page's lines — every one a chapter of this track: Stock value and trend (total and by room family — the capital headline, module 1's MD page matured); turns / cover (firm and per-branch, against the category bands — Ch. 2); aging profile (the strata, valued, with the 90+ line bolded — Ch. 3); dead stock value and ladder progress (the pipeline: entered, actioned per rung, released — Ch. 3's capital-release line); shrinkage rate (module 4's number, trend and distribution flags); expiry and markdown losses (module 3's horizon exhaust, by cause); availability rate (per class, with A-class bolded, and the month's stockout causes — Ch. 5); accuracy rate (module 4's certificate); and the exceptions line (open investigations, unclosed runs, negative flags — the aging exceptions from every module's machinery, counted). Twelve numbers, one page; every number drills to documents.

Targets and bands. Each line carries its target or band, set at implementation and reviewed annually: shrinkage under X%, A-availability over Y%, dead stock under Z% of holding, accuracy over W% — the numbers themselves are the client's to choose (with the consultant supplying trade norms and the arithmetic of each choice), but the CHOOSING is mandatory: a page without targets is a weather report; a page with them is a management instrument, because every line now reads green, amber, or a conversation.

The MD conversation, scripted. The page's monthly reading with the owner follows the same shape every time — which is its virtue: headline (the capital and its trend), the ambers (each with its owner's one-paragraph story and next action — the page holds people to narratives, not blame), the releases and saves (the ladder's line, the markdown that pre-empted a write-off, the availability point recovered — the wins made visible, because a page that only carries problems teaches people to dread it), and the ONE decision the month actually needs from the owner (the danger-quadrant review, the liquidation approval, the target reset). Twenty minutes; the owner leaves knowing their largest asset's condition; and the reading's regularity is what makes December boring — module 4's certificate, generalised to the whole system.

The page's owner. One name — the stock controller, the ops lead, the founder-until-delegated — who compiles (fifteen minutes, because every line is standing machinery), reads first, chases the ambers before the meeting, and owns the trends between meetings. The page without an owner joins Chapter 9's bestiary; the page WITH one is, for the stock system, what the run calendar was for the network: the heartbeat that makes everything else rhythmic. The final module hands this page its calendar slot and its place in the whole track's operating structure.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's health year
lessons.html:
The reading discipline, lived. Four quarters from first page to managed system — every chapter clocking in.

The first page (Ch. 1, 3, 7). Month one's compile is the shock the framing predicted: total stock ₦71m across the network... and the aging read's 90+ line holds ₦6.8m — 9.6% of the pool — that has not moved in a quarter, concentrated in three stories the value column tells at a glance: an over-bought vitamin range (the promo that under-performed), a branch allocation that shipped hope to Abeokuta, and a tail of 140 C-class SKUs dying quietly. The MD's first reaction is the classic — write it off? — and the consultant's reframe is the chapter's: this is capital in prison, and the ladder is the release programme, cheapest rungs first.

The ladder's two quarters (Ch. 3). Worked monthly, owned by name: PUSH recovers ₦900k at full margin (the hidden, not dead — front-shelf and counter suggestion did it); REBALANCE moves ₦1.1m of the Abeokuta allocation to where it sells (two laterals, priced and approved — module 6's machinery); MARKDOWN steps ₦2.3m through the pre-approved ladder (average recovery 71% of full price — against the write-off's zero); BUNDLE moves ₦400k of slow syrup riding the analgesic franchise; LIQUIDATE clears ₦200k of the C-tail to an institutional buyer at salvage. Two quarters in: ₦4.9m released, the 90+ line down to 2.8%, and the write-off rung needed for just ₦180k of genuinely dead stock — signed, coded, and fed upstream: the dead-stock cause read hands procurement two findings (the vitamin buy's quantity logic; the Abeokuta allocation's velocity assumption), and both planning fields are retuned.

The matrix repricing attention (Ch. 4). The quarter-two ABC refresh and the value-velocity matrix land on one page: 58 A items; the danger quadrant holds ₦9.4m across eleven items — nine of them deliberate (the specialty lines, documented as strategic holds with capped cover) and TWO of them drift (reviewed by name, cover halved, buying gated). The automation quadrant — 210 fast cheap SKUs — gets its planning fields tuned once and its counting lightened; the pruning quadrant's review delists 60 SKUs at the annual range review. Buying attention now follows the matrix, and the drift eye sharpens exactly where Chapter 4 pointed it.

Availability, lifted by placement (Ch. 5). The first availability read: A-class at 94.2% network-wide — but the DISTRIBUTION says the story: Central 98%, Ibadan 96%, Akure 89% — the new branch's fields still finding their level (module 6's day-90 retune, caught mid-flight). The stockout cause review runs monthly: two phantom-pipeline incidents (stale POs swept — Procurement 5's ritual now triggered from THIS read), one allocation short (policy-governed, relief-dated), the rest field-tuning. By quarter four: A-class at 98.1% — lifted not by holding more stock (total holding actually FELL ₦3.2m over the year as the ladder released and the fields tuned) but by placing it right: the placement dial, turned with both hands.

The year's page (Ch. 7). December's read: value ₦67.8m (down, deliberately — the capital released funded two months of the Akure expansion's stock); turns up 22% network-wide; dead stock 2.1% and pipelined; shrinkage 0.41% (module 4's steady state); A-availability 98.1%; accuracy 97.3%; every amber owned, every line three clicks from its documents. Twenty minutes with the MD, one decision (the next range review's date), and the sentence that closes the case study and sells the module: the reports didn't improve the stock — the reading did.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the seventh law
lessons.html:
The reading layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the firm-wide-only read. Symptom: healthy averages, dying branches; turns of 8 masking the item at 20 and the pallet at 0. Disease: rollup reading (Ch. 2) — the average of extremes hiding both diseases. Fix: distribution reads by construction — per item, per warehouse, exceptions against bands — the rollup reserved for the headline it honestly is.

Pattern 2 — dead stock as December's surprise. Symptom: the annual stocktake's write-off shock; the aisle pallet everyone stopped seeing. Disease: no threshold, no worklist, no ladder (Ch. 3) — slowness invisible until it is only a write-off. Fix: the written definition, the monthly aging read with owners, the ladder worked cheapest-rung-first, and the release framing that gets owners moving.

Pattern 3 — the invisible stockout. Symptom: lean, efficient... and quietly shrinking sales; customers drifting next door. Disease: the unrecorded failure (Ch. 5) — every visible number rewarding leanness, the punishing number never captured. Fix: zero-balance tracking and availability rates on the page, lost-sale capture at the counter, and the stockout cause review assigning fixes monthly.

Pattern 4 — the museum ABC. Symptom: counting and buying attention aimed by an analysis computed years ago; A-items of 2019 guarding the assortment of today. Disease: the structural reads never recomputed (Ch. 4). Fix: the quarterly refresh on the calendar, class changes read as news, the matrix rebuilt beside it.

Pattern 5 — the exported argument. Symptom: every management meeting runs on spreadsheets three exports old; numbers no one can trace; arguments that never end. Disease: the drill-down culture never built (Ch. 6) — figures detached from their documents living second lives as fiction. Fix: the reads interrogated in the system, provenance three clicks away, and the meeting discipline that any disputed number is opened live, not debated from tabs.

Pattern 6 — the ownerless page. Symptom: the health page compiled for three months, then quietly never again; targets unset; ambers unowned. Disease: the panel without its heartbeat (Ch. 7) — reading treated as a report, not a rhythm. Fix: one name, a calendar slot, targets chosen, and the twenty-minute MD reading that makes the compile matter — the final module's structure holds the slot.

The seventh law. The tree is the map; movements are documents; identity is operational; the count is a dialogue; valuation is written at the moment of movement; the network is one stock in many rooms. This module: stock health is read, not felt — the numbers exist the day the disciplines exist, and capital works exactly as hard as the rhythm that reads it. Turns ask if it's working, aging asks if it's moving, the matrix aims the attention, availability prices the empty shelf, and the page holds the panel to a heartbeat. One module remains: the structure that holds every rhythm, role, and rule this track has built — and hands the whole system to someone who isn't you.

advanced_inventory.title: Inventory 8 — Advanced Inventory: Settings, Roles & Structure
advanced_inventory.desc: The structural layer: Stock Settings as the constitution, the freeze and period discipline, item lifecycle governance, quality integration, the four stock authorities with the adjust permission's governance, the stock calendar, and the handover test — closing the track's eighth law.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Stock Settings: the warehouse constitution
lessons.html:
The final module of the final foundation track, and it opens where its siblings did: the settings screen, read as a constitution — because every default here is a policy the whole stock system will enforce silently, thousands of times, forever. The walk, field by consequential field, with the owner and the accountant in the room:

  • Allow negative stock — module 5's sternest conviction, now as configuration: OFF as default and discipline, ON only for the bounded, eyes-open exceptions (the go-live window, the deliberate fast-trade model with same-day posting) — and never, ever, flipped to silence an error message, because the message IS the control. The setting's review belongs to the annual walk; its emergency toggle belongs to nobody.
  • Default valuation method — the most consequential default in the stock system (module 5's words): the accountant's policy, chosen with the whiteboard conversation, applied consistently, changed only as a formal accounting event. The field encodes the decision; the walk is where the decision is confirmed to still be the decision.
  • UOM and conversion enforcement — the settings that make Buying 2's arithmetic structural: conversions validated at entry, the unit disciplines enforced where configuration allows, because the factor-of-twelve disease (module 4's count signatures) is cheapest to refuse at the field level.
  • Auto-creation toggles — the material-request automation switches (Procurement 3's machinery has its master switches here), batch and serial naming series (the identity system's registrar — series chosen once, at setup, with the same decade view as every naming decision).
  • The tolerance links — over-receipt and over-delivery allowances' global fallbacks (the gate numbers of both trading tracks, with their per-item overrides riding above).
  • Stock frozen up to — the period lock, important enough to own the next chapter whole.

The walk's discipline. As in both trading tracks: each field read as the policy question it is, the answers written into the implementation record, the annual re-walk on the calendar (the firm changed this year; did its constitution keep up?) — and the corridor toggle convicted one final time: a setting that keeps obstructing honest work is RETUNED in the walk, deliberately, with the owner; it is never flipped in the hallway to make one afternoon easier, because the hallway flip repeals the constitution for everyone to answer one letter. Three tracks have now taught this in three vocabularies; the consultant who holds it has a career's worth of prevented disasters that will never appear on any invoice.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The freeze: period discipline for stock
lessons.html:
The accounting close taught both money tracks that closed is closed; this chapter is the stock system's version — the machinery that makes the past stop moving.

Stock frozen up to. The setting names a date; stock entries dated on or before it are locked — no new postings into the frozen past, no edits to its truth — except by the ROLE the companion setting names (the narrow door: the accountant or controller who may, deliberately, post into frozen periods when the close's own corrections require it). The mechanics are simple; the discipline they enable is the point: module 5 showed how backdated entries recompute everything forward — valuations re-blend, COGS revises, reported figures move — and the freeze is how the firm draws the line behind which that may no longer happen casually: reported truth stays reported.

The monthly rhythm. The freeze advances with the close, as a ritual with an order: the month's stragglers swept IN first (the late paperwork posted with honest dates — the batched, announced sweep of module 5's governance, run deliberately before the door shuts); the reconciliations run (the stock-to-accounts bridge agreeing — module 5's certificate — plus the month's standing audits: the stock-entry review, the unallocated reads); THEN the frozen date advances to the month's end, and the period is closed in both systems at once — stock and accounts freezing together, because a stock period open behind a closed accounting period is an invitation for the two to diverge, and the bridge's whole job is that they never do. The close that runs this order takes an hour; the close that freezes first and sweeps after generates its own exceptions.

The narrow door's governance. The frozen-edit role is held by few (two names is a healthy number), its use is EVENTFUL (a posting into a frozen period carries its reason and its accountant-awareness — the module 5 boundary: closed-period entries are accounting decisions, not warehouse conveniences), and its usage is READ (the quarterly look at what went through the door, because a narrow door used weekly is a wide door with paperwork). The pattern to prevent is the freeze theatre: the date set once at go-live and never advanced (the lock that locks nothing), or advanced but with the edit role granted broadly (the lock with keys under the mat) — both leaving the past as editable as ever while the setting claims otherwise, which is worse than no freeze because it manufactures false assurance. The freeze that works is boring: advances monthly, guards absolutely, opens rarely, and logs when it does — the profile of every control this academy has built.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Item lifecycle governance: birth, change & retirement
lessons.html:
Modules 1-7 assumed items exist and behave; this chapter governs their LIVES — because the item master is the stock system's genome, and ungoverned item creation is how a clean implementation becomes a jungle in eighteen months.

Birth: the creation gate. Who may create items is a PERMISSION decision made deliberately: narrow (the controller, the master-data owner) for most firms, because every new item is a permanent commitment — a code, a UOM architecture, identity flags with their ten-year consequences (module 3), planning fields, tax templates — and the casually-created item gets all of these wrong at once. The gate's disciplines: the duplicate check first, always (search by every name the thing might wear — the jungle's dominant species is the same product under three codes, splitting its stock, its history, and its reorder logic three ways: the duplicate is not untidy, it is three lying bins wearing one product's face); the template discipline (item groups carrying defaults — new items born from their group's template inherit the architecture instead of improvising it); and the naming convention held (module 1's decade rule, item edition).

Change: amendment rights. The item's structural fields — UOM conversions, identity flags, valuation-relevant settings — are guarded harder than its descriptive ones, because structural changes on an item WITH history are events (the conversion changed under existing stock re-reads every quantity; the identity flag flipped is module 3's managed cutover, not an edit). The permission layer separates the two: descriptions and images broadly editable; structure behind the narrow door with the same eventfulness as frozen-period posting.

Retirement: the delisting flow. Items die too — the pruning quadrant (module 7) executed — and the flow is a sequence, not a click: open documents closed (no live orders or requests referencing it), stock cleared through the ladder's honest rungs (the item disabled with stock stranded is a bin nobody can act on), THEN disabled — out of every dropdown and search, history intact forever (never deleted: the ledger's testimony includes retired witnesses). The annual range review (module 7's pruning) feeds this flow its candidates; the flow's discipline is what keeps the assortment a decision instead of an accumulation.

Variants, briefly and honestly. Where products differ only by attribute — size, colour, strength — the variant machinery (one template, many variants) beats separate free-standing items: shared architecture, coherent reporting, one place to govern. The boundary judgment the consultant owns: genuine attribute families are variants; genuinely different products are items; and the wrong choice in either direction costs (variants stretched over different products entangle them; separate items for one product's sizes rebuild the duplicate jungle deliberately). The full variant machinery is its own study; this track's requirement is recognising the decision and making it at architecture time — the item chapter's ten-year view, one last time.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Quality integration: the inspection layer
lessons.html:
Quality has threaded through three tracks — the receiving fork, the pencil-whipped checklist, the batch quality notes. This chapter assembles the machinery into its structural form: inspections as configured, binding process.

The template. Per item (or item group), the Quality Inspection Template names the checks: parameters, acceptable ranges or criteria, reading types. The template is the quality standard MADE OPERATIONAL — the difference between check it properly (a wish) and a named list a person completes and signs (a control). Templates are written with whoever owns the standard (the pharmacist superintendent, the QA lead, the regulator's checklist transcribed) and versioned as standards change.

The binding points. Inspections attach where the flags say: at purchase receipt (the gate — Procurement 6's machinery: goods flagged inspection-required cannot be received into accepted stock without a completed inspection; the fork's evidence document); in-process (where repack or light production warrants a mid-flow check — the strips inspected before they join sellable stock); and at delivery (the outbound check for trades where what leaves must be verified — the serialized equipment powered on before dispatch, the export order's documented pre-shipment check). Each binding is proportionate by design: the flags sit on the items whose stakes warrant them (pharma actives yes, stationery no — the module 3 economics, quality edition), and the binding is REAL: where the flag is on, the document flow refuses to proceed without the inspection — the structural version of the discipline, which is the whole point of configuring it rather than requesting it.

The honest inspection. The pencil-whip conviction, final form: an inspection performed at the desk without the goods opened manufactures evidence of diligence not done — worse than no layer, because it converts YOUR OWN quality file into perjury. The defences are the audit family's: inspections spot-checked against reality (the QA lead re-opening a sampled carton against its filed inspection), inspection times read (the checklist completed in forty seconds was not performed), and the inspector's accountability framed as module 1 framed every custody — the signed inspection protects the honest inspector the day the batch goes wrong, because their diligence is on file.

The quality calendar and its reads. Quality's rhythms join the structure: inspection results trended (failure rates by supplier feeding the scorecard — Procurement 8's thread; by item feeding the spec conversations), quarantine's weekly review (the standing ritual, three tracks old), the disposal compliance file maintained (module 3's governed endings), and the annual template review (standards drift; checklists must follow). Quality integrated this way is not a department; it is a set of binding points in the same document flows everything else uses — which is exactly why it works at an 11-person firm: no quality team required, just flags, templates, and the calendar's eye.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Roles & the adjust permission: separating stock's authorities
lessons.html:
Both trading tracks separated their money authorities; stock's authorities are subtler and the stakes are the same. This chapter is the separation design — and the permission that deserves the module's sternest paragraph.

The four authorities. Across this track, four distinct powers have moved stock's truth: MOVE — transfers and stock entries (custody changing hands: the network's daily verbs); ADJUST — the reconciliation (truth OVERRIDDEN by count: the dialogue's final word); VALUE — rate-asserting documents (Material Receipts with typed rates, revaluations: money created or moved by assertion); and CONFIGURE — the settings, the item structure, the tree (the constitution itself). Each is a different kind of trust, and the design principle is the familiar one: the authorities CHECK each other only if they are separated — the person who moves stock daily should not casually hold the power to adjust the record their movements produce, and nobody's routine role includes rewriting the constitution.

The adjust permission — the eraser's license. Module 4 built the discipline (investigate, then adjust, in the open); this chapter builds its enforcement: the reconciliation permission is the most dangerous grant in the stock system, because it is the one document that overrides the ledger's computed truth with an asserted number — every other document ADDS truth; this one REPLACES it. Held broadly, it dissolves every control upstream: the custodian who can adjust their own custody can erase their own differences (the count's fairness dead), the shrinkage number reads whatever the adjusters left it (module 4's managed number, unmanaged), and the investigation discipline becomes optional the day everyone holds the eraser. The design: adjust held by TWO names (the controller and one senior backstop), never by warehouse operators, never by branch managers for their own branches (the self-adjustment ban is absolute — the custody and its correction never share a hand), with value thresholds routing large adjustments to a second sign-off even among the two. Every adjustment carries its investigation reference (module 4's file), and the monthly adjustments read — by author, value, warehouse, reason — is the permission's audit.

The rest of the map. MOVE: broad by necessity (the network runs on transfers) but shaped by module 1's warehouse restrictions (branch users to their leaves; van users to their vans) — the wrong choice made impossible, not just un-defaulted. VALUE: narrow (rate-asserting documents behind thresholds — modules 2 and 5's convictions as permissions). CONFIGURE: narrowest (settings, item structure, tree changes — the constitution's editors named, and few). And the sizing honesty, three tracks old: eleven people means hats share heads, but the irreducible core holds — the adjuster is not adjusting their own custody, the configurer's changes are eventful, and the two-names rule for the eraser survives every org chart, because it is two PEOPLE, not two departments.

Permissions enforce the design; they do not substitute for one. The closing principle from every structural module: the role matrix is the design made binding — and the design conversation (who SHOULD hold what, and why) is the deliverable; the matrix is its encoding. A permissions setup nobody can explain is a design nobody made.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The stock calendar: every rhythm, one page
lessons.html:
Eight modules installed rhythms; the consolidation, as ever, is the operating system. The stock function's recurring work, one page, with owners — the third and final calendar of the academy.

Daily. The exceptions scan: negative flags (counted same-day — module 5's drill), unclosed runs from yesterday (module 6), identity exceptions queued (module 3); the cycle counts (the day's lines, fifteen minutes — module 4); the van tailgates (evening reconciliation, every van, every day — module 6's smallest gate); and the bins read at the desks that trade on them.

Weekly. The transit review (runs closed, the room breathing, aging at zero — modules 2 and 6); the quarantine review (contents, reasons, next steps — three tracks' standing ritual); the expiry horizon (the worklist walked, ladder rungs assigned — module 3); the network dashboard (one page at the centre — module 6); and the branch weekly pages pushed out.

Monthly. The health page compiled, read with the MD, ambers owned (module 7); the stock-to-accounts bridge agreed (module 5); the stock-entry audit (purpose, value, author — module 2's boring page); the shrinkage and adjustments reads (module 4; Chapter 5's permission audit); the straggler sweep and the freeze advance (Chapter 2's ordered ritual); and the FEFO/override and identity exception reads (module 3).

Quarterly. The ABC and matrix refresh (module 7); the branch scorecards and reviews (module 6); the dead-stock cause read to procurement (module 7's letter); the allocation and lateral logs read (module 6's letters); the frozen-door usage read (Chapter 2); and the planning-fields exception review with buying (the joint ritual both tracks share).

Annually. The full count (module 4's production); the mock recall (module 3's drill, timed and filed); the tree review (module 1 — rooms without twins hunted both directions); the settings walk (Chapter 1); the range review feeding the delisting flow (Chapter 3); the quality template review (Chapter 4); and the calendar itself re-read — rhythms that earned their keep confirmed, decorations retired honestly.

The page's law, final statement. A rhythm without a name is a hope; the deliverable is this page WITH the names — sized to the firm (the eleven-person company's page has four names appearing often; the hundred-branch network's has a department), reviewed when people change, and treated as what it is: the stock function's entire operating system on one sheet. The consultant who leaves configured software has done half the job; three tracks have now said it, and the third saying is the summary: the calendar with owners IS the implementation — everything else is preparation for it.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The handover test: custody that survives its custodian
lessons.html:
The academy's deepest thread surfaces one last time: every structural module of every track has been building toward the same test, and stock — the function most often trapped in one trusted person's head — needs it most.

The test, stock edition. Could a competent newcomer, given what exists, run the warehouse function for a month with ZERO questions answerable only by the person who left? Walk what what exists must mean, module by module: the TREE tells them where stock can be and who answers for each room (1); the DOCUMENTS tell them how it moves and every movement's why (2); the IDENTITY system tells them what everything is, when it expires, and how to run the letter that might come (3 — the run-book on the shelf, drilled and timed); the COUNTING programme tells them what to verify and when, with the investigation discipline written (4); the VALUATION setup tells them what everything costs and forbids the shortcuts (5); the NETWORK playbook tells them the runs, the policy, the tailgates (6); the HEALTH page tells them what good looks like and where this month is amber (7); and THIS module's calendar tells them what to do every day, week, month, quarter — with the settings guarding the constitution while they learn. Every NO in the walk is a module incompletely done — the test is the audit, and the audit is the goal.

The storekeeper's path. The handover test read from the other side is a career ladder, and the consultant who frames it this way changes implementations: the CUSTODIAN (module 1's framing — answerable for a room, protected by documents, confirmed by counts) grows into the CONTROLLER (the adjust permission's holder, the calendar's owner, the health page's compiler) precisely BY the system existing — because a structured function has legible seniority (the clean-close streak, the accuracy rate, the owned rhythms are a promotion case written in numbers), while the unstructured one promotes whoever the owner trusts, which is a ceiling for everyone including the owner. The training deliverable that serves this: each role's slice of the calendar as their run-book, the disciplines taught as their protection (three tracks of that framing), and the path named — people keep disciplines that visibly lead somewhere.

The documentation set. The handover test passes on artifacts, and this track's are now enumerable: the opening file (module 4 — how the truth began), the tree and defaults record (1), the policy pages (allocation, thresholds, dead-stock definition, short-dating ladder — every written number the modules demanded), the run-books (recall, negative-stock drill, count production, van cycle), the calendar with names (6), and the settings record with its walk history (1-2). None of these is created FOR the handover; every one is a by-product of doing the modules properly — which is the academy's quiet thesis, stated once more: the system that runs well and the system that hands over well are the same system, and the founder-bottleneck (the concern that began these tracks' structural chapters) is solved not by finding a hero to trust but by building the structure a competent person can hold. The three-week absence, attempted deliberately before circumstance imposes it, is the test run in production — and the case study runs it.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: the structural year — and the graduate
lessons.html:
The final case study, in two acts: HealthTrade's stock function becomes structure, and the certification's graduate shows what three tracks buy.

Act one — the structural year. Q1, the constitution (Ch. 1-2): the settings walk with the MD and accountant — allow-negative confirmed OFF (the go-live window long closed), the method confirmed and recorded, frozen-upto instituted on the monthly rhythm with the ordered ritual (sweep, reconcile, advance), the narrow door held by the accountant and the ops lead. Q2, the incident and the narrowing (Ch. 5): the adjustments read flags a pattern — a branch supervisor with the reconciliation permission adjusting their own small variances, uninvestigated; nothing sinister found on review, but the design flaw is the finding: the eraser was distributed. The permission narrows to two names network-wide, the self-adjustment ban is written, and the next quarter's shrinkage read becomes honest for the first time (it RISES slightly — the differences previously erased now surface, investigate, and trend — the number getting worse because the truth got better, explained to the MD in exactly those words). Q3, item governance (Ch. 3): the creation gate catches a duplicate at birth — a new supplier's brand name for a paracetamol formulation already coded under its generic — merged before it splits a single bin; the annual range review feeds 60 delistings through the retirement flow, each cleared then disabled, history intact. Q4, the absence test (Ch. 7): the founder's three weeks abroad — the trading tracks passed their functions last year; this year the WAREHOUSE runs on its calendar, its run-books, and its two-name controls: twenty-one days, one incident (a transit shortfall, worked by the protocol, resolved from documents), zero founder-only questions. The handover test, passed by the function that used to live entirely in one storekeeper's memory.

Act two — the graduate (the academy's closing argument). A consultant holding all three certifications walks a prospect's warehouse — the distressed distributor from module 5's vignette — and reads it in a day, because every symptom now names its module: the flat sixty-warehouse tree (Inv 1), receipts at supplier-like rates (Inv 2's side door), batch fields empty on pharma lines (Inv 3 — the recall that cannot run), no count since the audit two years ago (Inv 4), allow-negative on since week two (Inv 5), branches buying retail from a network whose runs slip weekly (Inv 6 — and the diagnostic mercy: the branches are escaping, not rebelling), no page anyone reads (Inv 7), and every permission held by everyone (Inv 8). The findings deck writes itself in the modules' order; the remediation quote prices in the sequence module 5 taught; and the engagement it wins is delivered by the same curriculum run forward. That consultant — able to see a trading firm whole, from the supplier's master record to the branch's tailgate arithmetic to the naira of margin on the year's page — is what 24 modules, 216 lessons, and three certifications exist to produce. The academy's three tracks close where they began: with the conviction that a business runs on documents, masters, and rhythms — and that the professional who commands all three can walk into any trading firm in Nigeria and leave it structurally better than they found it.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Patterns, the eighth law & the track complete
lessons.html:
The structural layer's scar tissue, then the law that closes the track — and the academy's foundation.

Pattern 1 — the corridor toggle. Symptom: allow-negative on since an error message annoyed someone; frozen-upto never advanced; tolerances changed per complaint. Disease: the constitution edited casually (Ch. 1-2). Fix: settings behind the narrowest door, the annual walk as the only editing room, the corridor answered with the override paths every control provides.

Pattern 2 — the distributed eraser. Symptom: everyone adjusts; shrinkage reads suspiciously clean; the same custodies never vary. Disease: the reconciliation permission held broadly, self-adjustment unbanned (Ch. 5) — every upstream control dissolved by the one that overrides them. Fix: two names, the ban written, thresholds inside even the two, and the monthly adjustments read as the permission's standing audit — expecting shrinkage to RISE when the fix lands, and briefing the owner that worse numbers mean truer ones.

Pattern 3 — the duplicate jungle. Symptom: one product, three codes; stock, history, and reorder logic split three ways; nobody can say what the firm holds of anything. Disease: ungoverned creation (Ch. 3). Fix: the gate narrowed, the duplicate check mandatory, the templates carrying architecture, and the existing jungle merged deliberately — item by item, stock consolidated by document, the survivors' history preserved.

Pattern 4 — the freeze theatre. Symptom: the frozen date set at go-live and never moved, or moved with edit keys under every mat. Disease: false assurance manufactured (Ch. 2) — the past as editable as ever while the setting claims otherwise. Fix: the monthly advance in the close's ordered ritual, the narrow door with its usage read, and the theatre named for what it is.

Pattern 5 — quality theatre. Symptom: inspections filed in forty seconds; checklists perfect forever; the batch that fails in the market with a clean inspection on file. Disease: the pencil-whip at structural scale (Ch. 4) — the firm's own quality file converted to perjury. Fix: spot-checks against reality, inspection-time reads, and the inspector's protection framing that makes honesty the self-interested choice.

Pattern 6 — the unowned calendar. Symptom: rhythms that ran while the consultant watched and stopped when they left. Disease: the page without names (Ch. 6) — the implementation's second half never delivered. Fix: the calendar with owners as the closing deliverable, reviewed at every staffing change — and the follow-up visit that checks the rhythms, not the software.

The eighth law. The tree is the map of custody; stock moves only by documents; identity is operational; the count is a dialogue; valuation is written at the moment of movement; the network is one stock in many rooms; stock health is read, not felt. The eighth closes the track as its siblings closed theirs, because it is the same truth in its third and final vocabulary: custody that lives in structure — masters, documents, rhythms, and separated authorities — survives growth, turnover, and absence; custody that lives in a trusted head survives exactly as long as the head stays. The settings are the constitution, the freeze is the past's guardian, the adjust permission is the eraser licensed to two, the calendar is the heartbeat, and the handover test is the audit of all of it.

The track — and the foundation — complete. Eight modules: the map (1), the movements (2), the identities (3), the count (4), the money (5), the network (6), the reading (7), the structure (8). And with it the academy's third certification closes the foundation triad: Selling (money in), Procurement (money out), Inventory Management (the goods both of them move) — 24 modules, 24 laws, three continuous case studies, and one repeated conviction wearing every vocabulary the trade owns: documents over memory, masters over improvisation, rhythms over heroics, structure over trust. Take the assessment; then go read a warehouse.
